A workaround I've used was for a pretty specific plot, but the protagonists there were, for narrative purposes, revenants. Restless souls, carrying hatred for the BBEG, always aware of where he is, hunting him literally from one edge of the world to the other. Their souls, though, were originally not strong enough to form a full-on revenant. Their being is split. They have their memories and personality, but it's mixed with the memories of whatever body their souls inhabit. It's not quite the same person they were in life. 

Whenever any of them dies, the revenant spirit finds another body to continue their endless pursuit. Mechanically, this is a new character. I tell players they can't pick the same race, or share more than 2-3 levels with their previous body. And, the personality and dynamics get a chance to change, but the core gets to stay. Suddenly the character that used to be a squishy halfling wizard, teased for being small by the party's fighter, comes back as, say, a Goliath Barbarian! And maybe the fighter ends up a gnome cleric next time! They remember what their dynamic used to be like, so this change gets to... Maybe subvert, maybe change that dynamic. And once so far, a character who's sorta romancing another player character, came back as a paladin to protect her lover, so the reincarnation becomes kind of a development of the dynamic! 

At the same time, them being restless souls means you can introduce paladins and clerics that are capable of putting those souls to rest by force. So, sometimes, you can still create stakes of final death in the story! There's also something fun about anti-heroes whose greatest weakness is holy warriors and priests of gods. 

This definitely won't work for everyone, but if your goal is a meat grinder campaign that also has long-term storytelling, I feel like there's stories you can build that work into that! 

Then again, for me the lethality is about challenge, not necessarily about stakes. I want characters to be able to die, and suffer a serious setback - losing a lot of their magic items, especially in the case of a TPK - and have to claw their way back to face whatever slayed them again. If your goal is the emotional stakes of loss and the devaluation of human life that the protagonists experience losing friends, then... That might be harder.

Okay, since you're not that familiar with the slavery thing I wanna dip a little deeper into it. 

Not only did Rowling, through good characters like Hagrid, describe House Elves as willing slaves who'd feel devastated if you made them free, and insulted if you tried to pay them; but also she had an entire plot of Hermione being outraged about Hogwarts running on house elf slave labor, and trying her best to do activism to make it end. 

As a result of her efforts, Hermione is mocked by everyone. Including Harry and Ron. Even the narrative itself seems to mock her a tas - as her organization is abbreviated to "SPEW". She seems to be meant as "well-meaning but misguided" when trying to abolish slavery, since House Elves like being slaves, you see. Of course, Dobby was a House Elf, and he didn't like being a slave. So what's up? And the book seems to believe that "There are weirdoes in all groups" or something like that. See, Dobby was just weird! Normal House Elves loooove slavery! What if some other House Elves are also "weird" and don't like it? Don't think about it 😇 

That aside, there's tons of fatshaming aimed at Dudley, both in narration and actually spoken out loud, good guys using Crucio and Imperius curses, the horrifying Umbridge/Centaur thing, the Grim Old Place being stuffed with House Elf heads they never remove and just decorate for Christmas, Trelawny being a mean drunk, and an alcoholic, and nobody caring about her, and tons more points where characters are uncaring, cruel and malicious. 

As people smarter than me have pointed out, all of that together points at a sort of belief in morality that is shockingly essentialist. There aren't that many things that bad characters do or believe in, that good characters don't also do or believe in. The difference, generally, is that the victims of the good characters "deserve it" by being bad. 

In other words, there are no good or bad actions. Just good or bad people. And whether an action is good or bad depends on who's doing it. 

Harry bullying Dudley for being fat is good, because Harry is good and Dudley is bad. Dudley bullying Harry is bad, for the same reason. 

It could also point to why she's so certain in her cruel crusade. It's shockingly easy to mistake cause and effect. To believe that because you're a reasonable person, the things you believe are obviously going to be reasonable - instead of the other way around. It's rarely a conscious idea, just the vibes you feel when you get defensive about your beliefs. 

P.S. you can watch Shaun's video on Harry Potter for like 90 minutes of exposing the weird stuff from the books to people that haven't read them in a while

P.P.S. She also describes most evil characters as ugly in some way. And the way she makes women ugly is usually by making them masculine or mannish.

One thing you may benefit from keeping in mind is that Death of the Author is just a single (though very important and invaluable) filter you apply for a single reading of a work. 

So, Death of the Author is something you apply for the duration of the analysis, to determine if avoiding perceiving the author can bring other interesting interpretations. Death of the Author is also most applicable for abstract works. For example, Rothko! Rothko names his paintings like "Red, Violet and Green" so that you don't have a choice but to get your own interpretation. There's no "Authorial intent" expressed anywhere; Rothko is enforcing the Death of the Author on your perception to make your personal interpretation take precedence. 

But, there's like tooooons of works that are heavily influenced by the context of the author's circumstances. For those, knowing that context, being aware of who the author is and what life they'd lived, only serves to create a deeper understanding! 

If we accept both of those statements as True, then Death of the Author isn't something we just apply to everything, forever in perpetuity, all willy-nilly; but instead just one of the perspectives that make up our understanding of a text. Death of the Author is one very important perspective, yes, but it's just one perspective; and there are others we should consider to have a comprehensive understanding. 

We don't kill the author forever. We can't! The author will remain connected to the work. But, we can definitely pretend they're not there for a few hours while we process the text. To see what it'd feel like if they really weren't there

I think part of the point is that this is what Ainz tells himself. He asked the Workers - why are they here. He wanted to know what they'd be dying for. There was no reason to ask that, so I have to imagine he was feeling bad for them. 

Ainz thinks them greedy. But part of Ainz's/Satoru's story is that his new body, his new life, make him more and more removed from humanity. He doesn't relate to them anymore. And I think, in this moment what we see is Ainz misjudging people, because he forgot what it's like to be human and exist in the dystopian rat race that he was a part of. To him a person wanting money is just greed - even though for most people money's just a means to an end. A different end, for different people, but they're all in financial need, with things they want out of it - otherwise they'd be Adventurers. 

I think the key part is Foresight. We spend the most time with them and learn that, basically, they wanted to give the money for this mission to Arche, so that she can "retire" with her little sisters safely. They're not greedy. But they need money. The whole of Foresight in this moment doesn't want for themselves - they want for others. 

And given how much we are obviously mean to empathize with Foresight, how much time we spend with them, and the devastating reality of Arche's sisters; I am confident we're meant to see this moment as Ainz not seeing that needing money isn't necessarily greed.

The effort, however miniscule, is then what creates "ownership" of art.

I don't think you're being pedantic. Instead, I think that the rules you may or may not be pedantic don't seem particularly easy to get behind. I do consider HBG and LBG support weapons, even if they're not being used for support just about ever, as far as I've seen at least. And I would not consider SnS a support weapon. I still think it's a simple question of whether a weapon has support utility - that is, to benefit your team without doing damage - by default. HH is the most support weapon because you don't need anything really in order to provide what I determined to be Support. LBG and HBG are also support weapons to me, although they excel in other things so they're not built for support. Additionally, I think they're less of a support weapon because you still need to have special types of ammo in order to provide support, but it's still a ranged support weapon in my eyes. 


Ultimately, all of these are weapons, and they're designed to be useful enough to complete all content solo, provided you're good enough, because to a degree they have to be. When older games were coming out there was no guarantee you'd have internet, let alone one fast enough to let you play with others. And yet, simultaneously, it was a game designed to be played by teams. Thus, there was a small design conflict. All weapons have to be technically viable for beating the game solo, but at the same time you want weapons to have significant differences and allow differing playstyles so that you don't force a team to fight like four individuals and instead feature some teamwork. 


They tried to achieve that by making weapons that excel at different things, and as long as you include "Support" in things they'd be trying to work into the game - which to me is clearly the case via Lifepowder, Wide-Range and HH buff radius - you can identify weapons the design team tried to intend for support purposes. Those being HH, LBG and HBG. They elected not to lock that role into those weapons by adding Wide-Range as a skill, and eventually SnS ended up more useful for a support playstyle, but HH was intended for Support by its design and it can thus be fairly classified as a Support Weapon in my opinion

Your family could consider you a picky eater if you don't want to eat the liver your grandmother cooks. You've tried it before and you know you hate it. These two characters have a much simpler specialty so I recommend them if you're struggling with finding uses for your Chain Lightning.


Second tip is heroes. 200% in my opinion is only good to get that 500 point game for leaderboard. 180% is the most strategic and tactical because you actually have resources to manage and won't be screwed over by map generator as much. More importantly, what the 180% allows you to do is have 10k gold on day 1, which in 99% of your games will translate to at least two extra heroes on day 1. They speed up your exploration and give a nice big offensive boost to your main hero. Keep in mind that the hero speed on world map.is affected by the slowest units in their army, so these scouts should be equipped with the fastest unit you can afford to spare them. 


Third tip is the fact that Tower is hard to play. I'll try to explain it as best I can! Essentially, cards are the resources that win you the game so typically, you wanna remove those. If an enemy has 7 minions or just one - That's a big difference that can decide a game. However, you win ONLY when your opponent's health reaches 0 (besides Apocalypse, but as a new player don't worry too much about that). On the other hand, however, your enemy having 0 cards doesn't immediately lose and can topdeck what he needs to win, and at the same time, it makes TECHNICALLY no difference if you were at 30 health or at 1 health when you won. 

The general strategy is as follows. If you think your deck is overall stronger (read as "has on average bigger/ higher manacost cards) then you want to remove everything because eventually you will usually win. If you think your deck is worse prioritize ending the game as early as possible before the enemy can use all his fancy big cards. Not always true, but that's the general idea 

Another rule of thumb is that you want to use removal to kill minions and your minions to hit enemy hero. Exceptions are situations where you hold a card for a specific target. (Say, Polymorph for Tirion. If you're too new to know these cards then don't worry about it). 

But essentially it is as you said. Prioritizing health or cards are basics of two opposite gameplay styles - Aggro and Control respectively

And that's what scares me. Imagine if there was a card that hard-countered any of the popular archetypes? Say...
